name: Satoshi Nakamoto and the white paper
scope: The pseudonymous founder and the nine-page document that started Bitcoin. T1: on October 31 2008 (Halloween night), someone using the pen name SATOSHI NAKAMOTO posted a message to the CRYPTOGRAPHY MAILING LIST at metzdowd.com announcing 'a new electronic cash system that's fully peer-to-peer, with no trusted third party.' T2: attached was a nine-page paper titled 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact title). It contained no mathematics more advanced than probability theory -- deliberately readable by any competent programmer, not just cryptographers. T3: the CENTRAL PROBLEM the paper solves is called DOUBLE-SPENDING -- how do you stop someone from spending the same digital coin twice, WITHOUT a central authority (a bank, a PayPal) checking each transaction? Every digital-cash attempt before Bitcoin (DigiCash, e-gold) had needed a trusted issuer. T4: Satoshi's answer -- a PUBLIC TIMESTAMPED chain of transactions, with the ordering enforced by PROOF-OF-WORK computation, so that rewriting history would cost more energy than anyone could afford. Whoever has the most COMPUTING POWER working honestly wins the race to add the next block. T5: as of 2026 the REAL identity of Satoshi Nakamoto is still UNKNOWN -- despite hundreds of accusations, lawsuits, and forensic-text analyses. The person (or group) walked away from the project in 2011 and left roughly ONE MILLION bitcoins in early-mined addresses that have NEVER MOVED. Further rungs: the paper is 12 sections long (Introduction, Transactions, Timestamp Server, Proof-of-Work, Network, Incentive, Reclaiming Disk Space, Simplified Payment Verification, Combining and Splitting Value, Privacy, Calculations, Conclusion); the cryptography mailing list where it was posted was run by Perry Metzger and was a well-known cypherpunk-adjacent forum for reviewing cryptographic proposals.
source: PRIMARY: 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System' by Satoshi Nakamoto (bitcoin.org/bitcoin.pdf, 2008); the original metzdowd.com cryptography mailing list archive for October-November 2008. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Satoshi Nakamoto' and 'Bitcoin white paper' (2026-09-05) -- Halloween 2008 posting date, the metzdowd.com list, the ~1M untouched early-mined coins, the still-unknown identity as of 2026. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact wording of Satoshi's mailing-list announcement; the exact number of sections (12) in the paper.
framing_note: The FOUNDATION topic -- every kid who plays the game should meet Satoshi at T1 before any technical Bitcoin rung fires (teach-before-test). Dinner-test payoff: T5 (nobody knows who Satoshi actually IS -- one million coins sit untouched in his wallet, worth tens of billions of dollars, and he never came back). SCENE-LED: never 'What is Bitcoin?' -- always 'On Halloween night 2008 someone posted a nine-page paper to a cryptography mailing list.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: the SEEN was a paper about digital cash; the UNSEEN was that a solution to the double-spending problem meant money could exist without a central issuer -- the political implications only became visible over years. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem describes the SCENE (Halloween 2008, cryptography mailing list, nine-page paper, pseudonym) and the answer is the NAMED THING (Nakamoto, double-spending, proof-of-work, one million coins). ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT name any specific person as Satoshi -- Craig Wright's claim is legally rejected, Hal Finney explicitly denied it, all other attributions are speculation. DISTRACTOR MINE: other cypherpunk names (Hal Finney, Adam Back, Wei Dai, Nick Szabo -- real people who did related work), other digital-cash predecessors (DigiCash, e-gold, b-money, bit gold), other 2008-era financial events (Lehman collapse September 15 2008, TARP October 3 2008). CHOICE PARITY: if the answer is 'double-spending problem', distractors are other real cryptographic problems (Byzantine generals problem, zero-knowledge proof, RSA factoring).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the 2008 financial crisis as a political event; here the crisis is only the backdrop against which Satoshi published. SCIENCE owns cryptography-as-math (SHA-256 internals, elliptic curves) -- economics owns Bitcoin-as-monetary-engineering.

name: The genesis block and the Times headline
scope: The first block of the Bitcoin blockchain and the message Satoshi embedded in it. T1: on JANUARY 3 2009, Satoshi Nakamoto mined the very first block of the Bitcoin blockchain on his own machine. It is called the GENESIS BLOCK, or Block 0. T2: the block rewarded 50 BTC to a Bitcoin address -- which, uniquely, is UNSPENDABLE by a quirk of the original code (the reward can never be moved to another address). T3: inside the block's COINBASE TRANSACTION (the special first transaction that mints new coins), Satoshi embedded a line of text -- not a technical field, but a MESSAGE meant to be read: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact wording from the block chain). T4: that headline was the FRONT PAGE of The Times of London on the same day the block was mined. It served TWO purposes at once: (a) a TIMESTAMP proof -- the block could not have been mined earlier than 3 January 2009 because that headline did not exist yet; (b) a political statement -- Bitcoin was launching directly against the 2008 bank-bailout culture that had just seen the UK government preparing a second rescue of failing banks. T5: no fiat currency has ever been launched with a HEADLINE embedded in its founding document accusing the political class of debasing the money supply. The genesis block is the closest thing Bitcoin has to a DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE -- a founding text that names the enemy in one sentence. Further rungs: the block reward of 50 BTC never entered the circulating supply because of the code quirk; the next block (Block 1) was mined six days later, on January 9 2009, suggesting Satoshi paused to make sure the network worked before continuing.
source: PRIMARY: the Bitcoin block chain itself (Block 0, coinbase transaction raw hex, readable on any block explorer); The Times of London front page for January 3 2009. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Genesis block' and 'Bitcoin' (2026-09-05) -- January 3 2009 mining date, the coinbase-embedded Times headline as timestamp proof and political statement, the 50 BTC reward being unspendable, the ~6-day gap to Block 1. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact wording of the embedded headline text (spaces, punctuation) and the exact date of Block 1.
framing_note: The FLAGSHIP T5 payoff of the whole Bitcoin pillar -- kid learns that Bitcoin's founding document is itself a political act. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (the founder embedded a NEWSPAPER HEADLINE about bank bailouts inside the very first block, forever) and T4 (that headline serves as both the timestamp and the manifesto). SCENE-LED: the stem sets the scene -- 'On January 3 2009 the founder of Bitcoin mined the first block and hid a message in it' -- and the answer is what the MESSAGE said or what it PROVED. BASTIAT PATTERN check: this is a CYCLE RECOGNITION anchor -- Satoshi is pointing at the SEEN (a headline about a bank bailout) and inviting the reader to see the UNSEEN (that every bailout is paid by debasing the money of everyone who holds it). ACCURACY RAIL: the message is embedded in the COINBASE transaction, NOT in a comment or metadata field -- it is part of the immutable block data. The 50 BTC reward is unspendable due to a code quirk; do NOT say 'Satoshi chose to burn it' -- the technical reason is a script-hash mismatch in the original client. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem quote the headline and then ask what the headline said; describe the SITUATION (first block, embedded message, printed newspaper that day) and let the answer be the SUBJECT of the headline (bank bailout, the Chancellor, second rescue). DISTRACTOR MINE: other famous newspaper headlines from crisis moments (WALL STREET LAYS AN EGG 1929, DEWEY DEFEATS TRUMAN 1948, MEN WALK ON MOON 1969), other Bitcoin blocks with famous data (Block 170 -- first person-to-person transaction, Hal Finney; Block 78,357 -- pizza), other 'founding declarations' (Declaration of Independence, Magna Carta).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the 2008-09 bank bailout as a political event; economics owns why the bailout matters as a MONETARY event (debasement, moral hazard, Cantillon effect on the bailed-in banks' shareholders).

name: Satoshi's disappearance and the untouched million
scope: The pseudonymous founder walks away from his own creation. T1: from October 2008 until early 2011, Satoshi Nakamoto was ACTIVE -- posting on the bitcoin.org forums, emailing early developers, patching the code, and answering questions from cypherpunks and journalists. T2: his LAST PUBLIC FORUM POST was on DECEMBER 12 2010, on the bitcointalk.org forum, about DDoS defenses -- a technical, mundane message. He never posted publicly again. T3: his LAST KNOWN PRIVATE EMAIL was to the early Bitcoin developer MIKE HEARN on APRIL 23 2011 (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: date). In it he wrote 'I've moved on to other things. It's in good hands with Gavin [Andresen] and everyone.' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact quote wording). Then he vanished. T4: before disappearing, Satoshi had mined roughly ONE MILLION BITCOINS in the early days of the network, when he was often the ONLY miner running. Those coins sit in thousands of early addresses. AS OF 2026 they have NEVER MOVED -- not one satoshi. At any price above ~$50,000 per BTC, that hoard is worth more than fifty billion dollars, and yet it stays untouched. T5: the untouched million is the strongest evidence that Satoshi genuinely walked away. If he were alive and had access to the keys, he could have sold, borrowed against them, or moved them for privacy at any time in fifteen years. Instead, the coins sit as a KEPT PROMISE -- a founder who could have become the richest person on earth and simply DIDN'T. Further rungs: Gavin Andresen was the lead developer Satoshi handed off to; the last message on the forum used a normal signoff, giving no hint of the impending disappearance; the theory that Satoshi may have died is one possibility among several (illness, deliberate silence, prosecution fears), but none have ever been confirmed.
source: PRIMARY: the bitcointalk.org forum archive (Satoshi's post history and December 12 2010 final post); Mike Hearn's published emails from Satoshi. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Satoshi Nakamoto' (2026-09-05) -- December 12 2010 last forum post, April 23 2011 last email to Mike Hearn, the ~1M coins in early-mined addresses never spent, Gavin Andresen as designated successor. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact date of the final email to Hearn and the exact quoted wording of 'I've moved on to other things.'
framing_note: The T4/T5 payoff is the KEPT PROMISE -- a story kids can grasp immediately. Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the founder could have sold billions of dollars of his own creation, and CHOSE NOT TO for fifteen years). SCENE-LED: 'On December 12 2010 the founder of Bitcoin made an ordinary forum post. He never posted publicly again.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: this is an INCENTIVE RECOGNITION anchor at T5 -- Satoshi's non-selling REMOVED an incentive-conflict that would have plagued any other monetary founder (a central banker profits from inflation; a company founder profits from stock; Satoshi walked). ACCURACY RAIL: do NOT speculate on identity or motive as if it were fact -- 'as of 2026 nobody knows why' is the honest answer. Do NOT confuse Gavin Andresen (the successor Satoshi handed off to) with any of the false-Satoshi claimants. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem describes the SCENE (final forum post December 2010, final email April 2011, then silence for fifteen years) and the answer is a NAMED FACT (Mike Hearn, Gavin Andresen, one million BTC, 'I've moved on to other things'). Cooper), other 'founders who walked away' (Steve Wozniak leaving Apple, Andrew Grove retiring from Intel -- these did NOT vanish; distractors that TEACH), other early Bitcoin developers who did NOT vanish (Gavin Andresen, Mike Hearn, Hal Finney, Jeff Garzik).

name: Hal Finney: first node, first transaction, final letter
scope: The cypherpunk who ran the second Bitcoin node and became the movement's first martyr. T1: HAL FINNEY was a cryptographer at PGP Corporation who had spent the 1990s and 2000s working on privacy technology -- his name was on much of the code behind PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), the email encryption program used by journalists and dissidents worldwide. T2: on JANUARY 11 2009, days after the Bitcoin network went live, Finney downloaded the Bitcoin software and ran the SECOND-EVER Bitcoin node (Satoshi's own machine was the first). He tweeted 'Running bitcoin' -- one of the most famous two-word tweets in tech history. T3: on JANUARY 12 2009, Satoshi sent Finney 10 BTC -- the FIRST BITCOIN TRANSACTION between two different people (Block 170 on the block chain). Every other transaction until then had been Satoshi paying himself. T4: later in 2009, Finney was diagnosed with ALS -- amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the same disease as Lou Gehrig. It progressively paralyzed him. By 2013, when he wrote his final essay 'BITCOIN AND ME' on the bitcointalk.org forum, he was almost completely paralyzed and typing with eye-tracking software. He recounted running the second node, receiving the first transaction, and watching Bitcoin grow while his body failed. T5: Hal Finney DIED on AUGUST 28 2014. His body was CRYOPRESERVED by the ALCOR Life Extension Foundation in Arizona, per his long-standing arrangement -- Finney had been a life-extension advocate for decades. His BTC, held in cold storage, passed to his family. In the Bitcoin community he is remembered as the FIRST person besides Satoshi to see what Bitcoin was, and one of a small handful ever accused of being Satoshi (an accusation he denied and which the evidence has since ruled out). Further rungs: Finney's 'Reusable Proofs of Work' (2004) was one of the direct technical antecedents Satoshi cited; his forensic-text profile has been analyzed against Satoshi's and doesn't match; his son Jason Finney remains active in the Bitcoin community.
source: PRIMARY: Hal Finney's 'Bitcoin and me' post on bitcointalk.org (2013); his 'Running bitcoin' tweet January 11 2009; Block 170 on the Bitcoin block chain. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Hal Finney (computer scientist)' (2026-09-05) -- PGP career, running the second node January 11 2009, receiving the first person-to-person transaction (10 BTC in Block 170) on January 12 2009, ALS diagnosis 2009, 'Bitcoin and me' essay 2013, death August 28 2014, cryopreservation at Alcor, RPOW (Reusable Proofs of Work) 2004. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact date of his death; exact wording of the 'Running bitcoin' tweet.
framing_note: A HUMAN-STORY anchor in a technical pillar -- kids meet a real person, not an abstraction. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (he was preserved by Alcor because he genuinely believed the future might revive him -- Bitcoin was one of many long-view bets in his life). SCENE-LED: 'On January 11 2009, a cryptographer typed a two-word tweet.' 'On January 12 2009 he became the first person besides the founder to receive Bitcoin.' 'By 2013 he was typing with his eyes.' name: Proof-of-work and the digital lottery
scope: How Bitcoin secures itself with computation. T1: to add a new block of transactions to the Bitcoin block chain, a MINER's computer has to find a specific number, called a NONCE, that when combined with the block's contents produces a HASH (a scrambled fingerprint) starting with a certain number of zeros. T2: the only way to find such a number is TRIAL AND ERROR -- try one, hash it, check if it starts with enough zeros, if not try the next. Modern miners try TRILLIONS of guesses per second, per machine. T3: the analogy is a DIGITAL LOTTERY -- every guess is a lottery ticket, and the miner with the most tickets (the most hashing power) wins most often. Whoever finds the winning nonce broadcasts the block, and other miners immediately switch to building on top of it. T4: the ENERGY spent on this is NOT WASTE -- it is what makes Bitcoin trust-minimizing. To rewrite the block chain (say, to steal), an attacker would need to REDO all the proof-of-work of every block they want to rewrite, faster than the honest network can extend the chain. That means the attacker would need MORE than half the world's Bitcoin hashing power -- and would have to keep spending that energy every second. The energy IS the security. T5: this design is called NAKAMOTO CONSENSUS -- named for Satoshi. It is the first known solution to what computer scientists call the BYZANTINE GENERALS PROBLEM: how do untrusted, distributed parties reach agreement on a shared record without any central authority. Every Bitcoin block is a fresh, verifiable proof that real-world electricity was burned to secure the network -- which is why critics who call Bitcoin 'wasteful' are missing the point, and defenders reply that fiat currencies also cost energy (bank branches, armored trucks, printing, the entire regulatory apparatus) that is simply less visible. Further rungs: the hash function Bitcoin uses is SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output); the required number of leading zeros is set by the DIFFICULTY, which the network adjusts every 2,016 blocks; the specific reward for finding a valid block is called the BLOCK REWARD.
source: PRIMARY: the Bitcoin white paper (Sections 4 Proof-of-Work and 5 Network); the Bitcoin source code (miner.cpp and its documentation). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Proof of work' and 'Bitcoin mining' (2026-09-05) -- SHA-256 as the hash function, nonce search, difficulty target, the Byzantine Generals problem framing, Nakamoto Consensus as a named contribution, the energy-as-security argument. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: current hash rate figures if used (they change fast); the exact hash function name (SHA-256).

Dinner-test payoff: T4 (the electricity Bitcoin burns is not waste -- it is the WALL that protects every dollar of value on the network). Never call Bitcoin's proof-of-work 'wasteful' as if it were settled -- present the debate as a debate and let the answer be the honest reasoning move on either side. NO code, NO cryptographic math beyond 'a hash is a scrambled fingerprint'. name: The halving and the 21 million cap
scope: Bitcoin's hard-coded scarcity schedule. T1: every time a miner adds a block to the Bitcoin block chain, they are rewarded with NEWLY CREATED bitcoins. In 2009, that reward was 50 BTC per block. T2: every 210,000 BLOCKS -- which works out to roughly EVERY FOUR YEARS -- the reward is CUT IN HALF. This event is called the HALVING (or 'halvening' in early forum slang, though 'halving' won). T3: the schedule so far: 50 BTC (2009), 25 BTC after the first halving (November 2012), 12.5 BTC (July 2016), 6.25 BTC (May 2020), 3.125 BTC (April 2024), 1.5625 BTC (expected 2028). Each halving is a scheduled, non-negotiable code event visible in the Bitcoin software from day one. T4: because each halving cuts issuance in half, the TOTAL SUPPLY converges on a mathematical limit -- 21 MILLION bitcoins, expected to be reached around the year 2140. After that, miners will earn only TRANSACTION FEES, not new coins. T5: this fixed 21-million cap is the sharpest possible contrast with FIAT currency, whose supply can be expanded at will by a central bank. Milton Friedman famously said 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon' -- meaning it is caused by growing the money supply. Bitcoin is the first known form of money whose supply CANNOT be expanded, by anyone, ever -- no committee, no politician, no emergency. Whether that is a virtue or a bug is the whole debate between Austrian sound-money advocates and Keynesian aggregate-demand advocates. Further rungs: the smallest unit of Bitcoin is called a SATOSHI (1 BTC = 100 million satoshis); the halving schedule was designed by Satoshi as a geometric series that could never be altered without breaking every wallet on the network; the 2140 completion date is an approximation based on the average 10-minute block time.

CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact dates of each past halving; the current 2026 block reward (3.125 BTC after the April 2024 halving).

What is this scheduled event called?' or 'Around the year 2140, something happens that has never happened to any currency before.' Do not present the cap as a prediction; it is a rule enforced by every node running the reference software. name: Difficulty adjustment: the homeostatic clock
scope: How Bitcoin keeps its heartbeat steady regardless of how many miners are competing. T1: Bitcoin is designed to have a new block added about EVERY TEN MINUTES on average. Not every ten minutes exactly -- some blocks come in one minute, some in thirty -- but the AVERAGE across many blocks is ten minutes. T2: if a lot of new miners join the network with powerful machines, blocks would start arriving FASTER than every ten minutes. If miners quit and hashing power drops, blocks would arrive SLOWER. Either would break the halving schedule and the security model. T3: every 2,016 BLOCKS (about two weeks at ten minutes each), every Bitcoin node automatically checks: how long did those 2,016 blocks actually take? If they came in fast, the DIFFICULTY is turned UP (miners must find hashes with more leading zeros); if slow, difficulty is turned DOWN. This is the DIFFICULTY ADJUSTMENT. T4: this makes Bitcoin's monetary policy HOMEOSTATIC -- like the way your body keeps its temperature at 37 degrees whether it is winter or summer. No committee, no vote, no press conference; the network self-corrects. T5: the biggest real-world test came in 2021, when China's government BANNED Bitcoin mining in June 2021 and roughly HALF the world's hashing power went offline in weeks. Blocks slowed dramatically. But at the next scheduled difficulty adjustment, the network automatically dropped the difficulty by about 28 percent -- the largest downward adjustment in Bitcoin's history -- and blocks returned to a normal ten-minute cadence. Meanwhile, the fleeing Chinese miners physically relocated to Texas, Kazakhstan, and Paraguay, and hashing power recovered to a new all-time high within nine months. Further rungs: the difficulty is stored in every block header as a 32-bit field called 'bits'; the 2,016-block period is exactly two weeks IF blocks come in every 10 minutes; the biggest UPWARD adjustments have happened in bull markets when new mining hardware ships in large batches.

name: ASIC evolution: CPU to specialized silicon
scope: How Bitcoin mining hardware evolved from ordinary computers to purpose-built machines. T1: in 2009 and 2010, everyone mined Bitcoin on their ordinary CPU -- the general-purpose chip inside every laptop and desktop. Satoshi did. Hal Finney did. Anyone could. T2: in late 2010, developers realized that a computer's GRAPHICS CARD (GPU) -- a chip designed to render video-game pixels -- was FIFTY to a HUNDRED TIMES faster at Bitcoin hashing than a CPU. The gamers' hardware was accidentally the world's best money-mint. GPUs dominated 2010-2011. T3: in 2011, mining moved to FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array) chips -- reconfigurable hardware faster than GPUs but expensive. FPGAs were a bridge; they only lasted about a year. T4: in 2013, the first ASIC arrived -- an APPLICATION-SPECIFIC INTEGRATED CIRCUIT designed for one job only: computing SHA-256 hashes as fast as physics allows. ASICs immediately obsoleted every CPU, GPU, and FPGA miner overnight. Butterfly Labs, Avalon, and later BITMAIN made the first generations. T5: today, mining is DOMINATED by a small number of manufacturers -- Bitmain's Antminer series, MicroBT's Whatsminer, and Canaan's AvalonMiner -- each shipping million-machine batches to industrial mining farms. The economics: an ASIC is USELESS for anything else; it can only hash SHA-256. That means every miner who buys one is committed to Bitcoin's success -- selling the machine as scrap or Bitcoin cash-flow are the ONLY options. Critics called this centralization; defenders call it commitment. Further rungs: post-ASIC coins (Kaspa, Alephium) have tried alternative proof-of-work hashes designed to resist ASIC dominance; Bitmain was founded by Jihan Wu and Micree Zhan in 2013 in Beijing; the largest mining farms today are in Texas (post-2021 China exodus), Iceland (cheap geothermal), and Paraguay (Itaipu Dam hydro).

name: Mining pools: from solo miners to global cooperatives
scope: How mining moved from lone hobbyists to organized pools. T1: in 2009 and early 2010, mining Bitcoin was a solo activity -- run the software on your laptop, and once every few days you might find a block and win 50 BTC. As more miners joined, the odds of any one solo miner ever finding a block dropped toward zero. T2: in NOVEMBER 2010, a developer using the handle SLUSH set up the first MINING POOL -- a system where many miners combine their hashing power and split the rewards proportionally to the work each contributed. It was called Slush Pool (now Braiins Pool). T3: a pool works like this: a coordinator collects hashing effort from thousands of miners, submits blocks under a single pool address when won, and pays each miner in proportion to how many valid partial-hashes they contributed. Instead of one big lucky payout every few years, a miner gets a small steady stream of Bitcoin every day. T4: today the top pools (rotating list of about six) collectively control most of the world's hashing power: FOUNDRY USA (owned by Digital Currency Group, US-regulated), ANTPOOL (Bitmain-affiliated), F2POOL (China-origin, now Singapore), VIABTC, BINANCE POOL, and Slush/BRAIINS POOL as the pioneer. T5: this concentration creates the '51% ATTACK' concern -- if any single pool ever gained more than half the network's hashing power, it could theoretically rewrite recent history or block chosen transactions. In practice, when GHash.io briefly exceeded 51% in JULY 2014, miners voluntarily left the pool to lower its share and preserve the network -- a demonstration that pool operators know their power depends on user trust. name: Self-custody and 'not your keys, not your coins'
scope: The Bitcoin community's hardest-won lesson. T1: Bitcoin is CONTROLLED by whoever holds the PRIVATE KEY -- a specific number that, when signed against a transaction, proves ownership. Without the private key, the coins cannot be moved. With it, they can. T2: when you keep Bitcoin on an EXCHANGE (Coinbase, Kraken, Binance), the exchange holds the private keys for you. You have an IOU from the exchange; you do NOT have the coins. If the exchange freezes accounts, goes bankrupt, or is hacked, you may lose everything. T3: the phrase 'NOT YOUR KEYS, NOT YOUR COINS' was popularized by ANDREAS ANTONOPOULOS, a Greek-British Bitcoin educator and author of Mastering Bitcoin. It is the community's shortest possible statement of the self-custody principle. T4: to hold your own keys, you use a WALLET that stores them. Best practice uses a HARDWARE WALLET -- a small dedicated device (Trezor from Czechia, Ledger from France, Coldcard from Canada) whose keys never touch an internet-connected computer. The BACKUP is a SEED PHRASE: 12 or 24 English words defined by BIP39 (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 39), which can regenerate every key even if the device is destroyed. Written on paper or stamped in steel, hidden in different places. T5: the lesson has been taught twice by history at massive scale. FEBRUARY 2014: the Mt Gox exchange collapsed with ~850,000 BTC lost or stolen -- roughly 7% of all Bitcoin ever mined at the time. NOVEMBER 2022: the FTX exchange collapsed with billions of customer dollars missing, its founder Sam Bankman-Fried later sentenced to 25 YEARS in prison. Every FTX customer who had held self-custody was fine; every customer who had trusted the exchange lost access. THE SAME LESSON, EIGHT YEARS APART. Further rungs: hardware-wallet operations happen offline (COLD STORAGE); a 'multisig' arrangement requires several keys signing to move funds; the seed phrase is human-readable so it can be recovered without any specific vendor's software.

name: Lightning Network: micropayments on top of Bitcoin
scope: The layer-2 payment system that lets Bitcoin scale to coffee-sized transactions. T1: the Bitcoin base layer confirms about ONE BLOCK EVERY TEN MINUTES, with a hard limit on how many transactions each block can hold -- typically a few thousand per block. That is fine for large transfers, but too slow and too costly for buying a coffee. T2: the LIGHTNING NETWORK is a second layer built on top of Bitcoin. Instead of putting every transaction on the block chain, users open a PAYMENT CHANNEL -- a shared funding transaction between two parties -- and can then send Bitcoin back and forth INSTANTLY, hundreds of times, without touching the block chain. Only the opening and the eventual closing of the channel are recorded on-chain. T3: channels connect into a NETWORK -- if you have a channel with Alice, and Alice has a channel with Bob, you can pay Bob through Alice without any of you having a direct channel to everyone. Small fees compensate the routing nodes. T4: Lightning was proposed by JOSEPH POON and THADDEUS DRYJA in a 2016 white paper. The mainnet went live in MARCH 2018 (CORROBORATE AT BUILD). User-facing apps include STRIKE (Jack Mallers), WALLET OF SATOSHI (custodial, easy for beginners), and PHOENIX (self-custodial). T5: the most visible real-world deployment was EL SALVADOR's CHIVO WALLET, launched September 7 2021 alongside Bitcoin becoming legal tender there. Small merchants could accept Bitcoin over Lightning for the price of a pupusa -- a transaction that on the base layer would have been uneconomic in fees. Lightning's design is not perfect (channel management, liquidity, watchtowers for security), but it demonstrates that Bitcoin can be BOTH a settlement layer for large transfers AND a payment network for small ones -- similar to how the internet has TCP/IP at the base and higher-level protocols on top. Further rungs: routing payments requires enough liquidity along a path; the largest public Lightning nodes are run by exchanges and payment processors; a watchtower is a service that watches a channel while you are offline in case your counterparty tries to close it dishonestly.

name: Silk Road: Bitcoin's first widely-known use case
scope: The Tor-hidden marketplace that put Bitcoin on the front page for the first time. T5: Ulbricht's sentence became a cause celebre in libertarian, criminal-justice-reform, and Bitcoin circles for a decade -- his defenders argued the life-without-parole sentence for a first-time non-violent offense was disproportionate; his prosecutors argued the market's scale (~$1.2 billion in sales) and unproven murder-for-hire allegations warranted it. name: El Salvador: the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender
scope: The Central American country that made Bitcoin legal alongside the US dollar. T1: on SEPTEMBER 7 2021, EL SALVADOR became the FIRST COUNTRY IN THE WORLD to make Bitcoin LEGAL TENDER -- meaning by law it must be accepted for payment of any debt, alongside the US dollar (which had been El Salvador's official currency since 2001). T2: the law was driven by President NAYIB BUKELE, a young populist president elected in 2019. Bukele announced the plan at a Bitcoin conference in Miami in JUNE 2021 (Bitcoin 2021 at the Wynwood convention center), then pushed the Bitcoin Law through the Salvadoran Legislative Assembly within days. T3: alongside legal tender, the government rolled out CHIVO WALLET -- a national mobile-phone wallet that used the Lightning Network so small merchants could accept Bitcoin without heavy on-chain fees. Every adult Salvadoran was offered $30 in Bitcoin as a signing bonus to download the app. T4: the INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND (IMF) publicly opposed the move, arguing that Bitcoin's price volatility posed 'macroeconomic risk' and pressed El Salvador to reverse course -- particularly during 2022 loan negotiations. El Salvador refused. Bukele publicly mocked the IMF on Twitter and continued the policy. T5: over 2021-2024, El Salvador ACCUMULATED Bitcoin as a national reserve, adopting a policy of buying 1 BTC per day. Bukele made the policy a national identity marker -- new tourism, a proposed 'Bitcoin City' near the Conchagua volcano powered by geothermal energy, and El Salvador as a Bitcoin-tourism destination. Whatever the long-run economics, the ACT was historic: the first time in modern history any country had legalized a non-state, unforgeable monetary asset as tender, in direct defiance of the international-financial-institution consensus. Further rungs: El Salvador dropped the Bitcoin-legal-tender requirement to a permissive-tender rule in early 2025 as part of an IMF deal (CORROBORATE AT BUILD); the Chivo wallet had significant early bugs and adoption resistance; some rural areas continued to use dollars almost exclusively.

name: The white paper's twelve sections
scope: The structure of the founding document. T1: Satoshi's white paper is nine pages long and organized into TWELVE numbered sections. It is exactly the length of a computer-science conference paper of its era. T2: the twelve sections in order are: (1) INTRODUCTION -- states the double-spending problem and previews the peer-to-peer solution. (2) TRANSACTIONS -- defines a coin as a chain of digital signatures. T3: (3) TIMESTAMP SERVER -- introduces the concept of a timestamped chain of blocks. (4) PROOF-OF-WORK -- Adam Back's Hashcash idea adapted to secure the timestamp chain. (5) NETWORK -- how nodes propagate transactions and blocks. T4: (6) INCENTIVE -- why miners honestly follow the protocol (block reward + fees). (7) RECLAIMING DISK SPACE -- the Merkle tree structure that lets old transaction data be pruned. (8) SIMPLIFIED PAYMENT VERIFICATION (SPV) -- how a light client can verify payments without downloading the full chain. T5: (9) COMBINING AND SPLITTING VALUE -- how a transaction can have multiple inputs and outputs, the model most Bitcoin transactions still use. (10) PRIVACY -- how anonymity can be preserved by separating identity from public keys. (11) CALCULATIONS -- the probability math showing why an attacker with less than 50% of hash rate will lose. (12) CONCLUSION -- a two-paragraph summary. Further rungs: the paper cites eight prior works, including Adam Back's Hashcash and Wei Dai's b-money; the Introduction opens with the line 'Commerce on the Internet has come to rely almost exclusively on financial institutions serving as trusted third parties to process electronic payments.' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD); the paper's abstract fits on one page.

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin white paper' (2026-09-05) -- 9 pages, 12 sections in the order given, references to Hashcash and b-money among the 8 citations. name: The cypherpunk lineage: DigiCash, b-money, Hashcash, bit gold
scope: The four major digital-cash proposals that came before Bitcoin. T1: the CYPHERPUNKS were a mailing-list movement of the 1990s -- cryptographers and privacy advocates who wrote 'The Cypherpunk Manifesto' (Eric Hughes 1993) and pursued the goal of making cryptographic tools that would secure individual privacy against surveillance. Wei Dai, Hal Finney, Adam Back, Nick Szabo, and Julian Assange were all connected to this community. T2: DAVID CHAUM's DIGICASH (founded 1989) implemented BLIND SIGNATURES -- a cryptographic technique letting a bank issue anonymous digital cash. Users could spend money without the bank knowing who spent it, while the bank still controlled issuance. DigiCash filed for bankruptcy in 1998 -- ahead of its time and unable to find bank partners. T3: WEI DAI's B-MONEY (proposed November 1998, in a cypherpunk mailing-list post) sketched a decentralized digital cash where transactions were broadcast to a network and each participant kept a ledger. B-money was never implemented -- it was a design essay. Satoshi cited it explicitly in the Bitcoin white paper. T4: ADAM BACK's HASHCASH (published 1997) invented PROOF-OF-WORK -- originally as an anti-spam measure for email. To send email, a sender had to compute a small hash puzzle, imposing a cost that made mass-spam economically unviable. Bitcoin adopted the same hash-puzzle technique to secure its block chain. Back is British, later founded Blockstream, and remains a major Bitcoin developer. T5: NICK SZABO's BIT GOLD (proposed 1998, blog post 2005) was the CLOSEST precursor to Bitcoin -- a design where computers competed to solve proof-of-work puzzles, the solutions were chained together in a timestamped registry, and the resulting scarce digital units functioned as money. Bit gold was never built. Szabo (whose linguistic style is one of the reasons some suspected him of being Satoshi -- an accusation he has denied) has written extensively on smart contracts and monetary theory. Bitcoin is best understood as the SYNTHESIS of all four proposals -- DigiCash's cryptographic elegance, b-money's decentralization, Hashcash's proof-of-work, bit gold's scarcity model. Further rungs: Bitcoin cites b-money and Hashcash in its references but not DigiCash or bit gold explicitly; the Cypherpunk Manifesto opens 'Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age'.
source: PRIMARY: Wei Dai 'b-money' (cypherpunk mailing list, November 1998, archived at weidai.com/bmoney.txt); Adam Back 'Hashcash - A Denial of Service Counter-Measure' (2002 paper); Nick Szabo 'Bit Gold' (2005 blog post); David Chaum 'Blind Signatures for Untraceable Payments' (1982 paper, DigiCash founded 1989). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Cypherpunk', 'DigiCash', 'Hashcash', 'Bit gold', 'Wei Dai' (2026-09-05) -- Chaum's blind signatures and DigiCash 1989-98, Wei Dai's November 1998 b-money proposal, Back's 1997 Hashcash, Szabo's 1998 bit gold, all cited or paralleled in the Bitcoin white paper. name: Halving cycles and market patterns
scope: The observable four-year pattern in Bitcoin's market history. T1: Bitcoin's price history shows a rough FOUR-YEAR CYCLE that observers have tied to the halving schedule. Each halving cuts new-Bitcoin issuance in half; supply pressure adjusts; demand catches up; a bull market ensues; a bear market follows; the cycle repeats. T2: the OBSERVED PATTERN across cycles: 2011 first mini-bull (peak ~$30); 2013 bull (peak ~$1,100 late in year -- roughly one year after November 2012 halving); 2017 bull (peak ~$20,000 December -- roughly 18 months after July 2016 halving); 2021 bull (peak ~$69,000 November -- roughly 18 months after May 2020 halving); 2024-25 cycle (breaking $100,000 December 2024 -- roughly 8 months after April 2024 halving, driven partly by spot-ETF flows). T3: the FOUR PHASES analysts describe: (1) BEAR / CAPITULATION -- price collapsed from prior peak, weak hands sold, sentiment terrible. (2) ACCUMULATION -- price flat, quiet buying by long-term holders. (3) MARKUP -- price rises, awareness returns. (4) DISTRIBUTION / EUPHORIA -- price parabolic, retail piles in at the top, cycle turns. This is a classic AUSTRIAN BUSINESS CYCLE shape applied to a monetary asset. T4: Austrian analysts (like Bitcoin-native writers Vijay Boyapati, Lyn Alden, Saifedean Ammous) argue that these cycles are a MONETARY phenomenon in Bitcoin's early-adoption phase -- reflecting the supply-shock impact of halvings combined with expanding institutional demand curves. As adoption matures, cycles may soften. T5: the CRITICAL CAUTION: past cycles do NOT guarantee future cycles. The 2024-25 cycle has already diverged from prior cycles in speed and character (ETF-driven demand, corporate treasury adoption, sovereign accumulation). Every prior cycle looked in retrospect like a pattern; every next cycle might not follow it. This is a case where the RECOGNITION of the historical pattern is teachable, but the FORECAST is speculative and the bank should not present it as a certainty. Further rungs: the cycle-lows have historically been higher than the previous cycle-lows (a rising floor); the 'stock-to-flow' model by an anonymous analyst 'PlanB' claimed to predict prices from the halving schedule but has largely FAILED as a forecast tool since 2021 -- teach as cautionary tale, not endorsement.

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Bitcoin' and cycle-related articles (2026-09-05) -- observed halving-adjacent bull cycles 2013, 2017, 2021, 2024-25; the four-phase market cycle description common in Austrian and technical-analysis writings; the stock-to-flow model's high-profile failure since 2021. name: SegWit and Taproot: the two big soft forks
scope: The two most significant protocol upgrades in Bitcoin's history. T1: Bitcoin can be upgraded through SOFT FORKS (backward-compatible upgrades that old nodes still accept) or HARD FORKS (breaking upgrades that split the network). Soft forks are preferred because they preserve consensus. T2: SEGWIT (Segregated Witness) activated on AUGUST 24 2017 after years of contentious debate. It restructured transaction data so that the signature (the 'witness') was moved outside the main transaction body -- freeing up block space and fixing a subtle technical issue called transaction malleability. T3: the SegWit debate was called the BLOCK SIZE WAR -- some in the community wanted to increase Bitcoin's block size directly to allow more transactions per block; others wanted SegWit's more elegant approach. The dispute led to a HARD FORK in August 2017 that created BITCOIN CASH (BCH) as a separate, larger-block-size cryptocurrency. Bitcoin (BTC) itself adopted SegWit. T4: TAPROOT activated on NOVEMBER 14 2021 -- the largest Bitcoin upgrade since SegWit. Taproot bundled several improvements: SCHNORR SIGNATURES (more efficient and privacy-preserving than the older ECDSA signatures), improved MULTI-SIGNATURE capabilities, and better SMART CONTRACT flexibility while keeping Bitcoin's conservative security posture. T5: Taproot's activation was NOTABLY DRAMA-FREE compared to SegWit. Over 90% of mining hash power signaled support during the 'Speedy Trial' activation period June-August 2021, and the upgrade activated smoothly in November. This showed that Bitcoin's upgrade process could work when the community was aligned -- a demonstration that decentralized consensus could deliver careful technical progress without factional civil war. Further rungs: 'Ordinals' -- a way of inscribing arbitrary data on individual satoshis -- was enabled unintentionally by Taproot in January 2023, becoming both a use case and a debate; the block-size war produced multiple books, notably Jonathan Bier's 'The Blocksize War' (2021); Bitcoin's culture of conservative upgrades stands in sharp contrast to Ethereum's frequent forks and design changes.

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'SegWit', 'Taproot', 'Bitcoin Cash', 'Block size war' (2026-09-05) -- SegWit August 24 2017 activation, Bitcoin Cash August 1 2017 fork, Taproot November 14 2021 activation, Schnorr signatures, the block-size war history. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact activation dates.

Dinner-test payoff: T3 (Bitcoin's community had a CIVIL WAR over how to upgrade, and one side left to create a separate coin -- BITCOIN CASH) and T5 (Taproot showed the process could work smoothly when the community was aligned). name: Proof-of-work vs proof-of-stake: the Ethereum Merge
scope: The other main consensus mechanism and why Bitcoiners argue it's inferior. T1: PROOF-OF-STAKE (PoS) is an alternative to proof-of-work in which the right to add the next block is not earned by burning electricity, but assigned by STAKING an amount of the cryptocurrency itself as collateral. Whoever stakes more has a proportionally higher chance of being chosen to add the next block. T2: PoS supporters argue it is ENERGY EFFICIENT (no massive electricity use), FASTER (blocks can come in seconds), and equally secure. PoS critics -- especially Bitcoiners -- argue it is a return to a PERMISSIONED model in disguise: whoever starts with the most tokens has the most power to add blocks, entrench themselves, and shape the network, without any external check equivalent to the work required in proof-of-work. T3: on SEPTEMBER 15 2022, ETHEREUM completed 'THE MERGE' -- a scheduled transition from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake. This was one of the largest software upgrades ever performed on a live financial network, and technically it went smoothly. Ethereum's energy consumption dropped by roughly 99.95 percent overnight. T4: the BITCOIN COMMUNITY's response was mostly critical. Arguments: (a) PoS requires trusted checkpoints to prevent 'nothing-at-stake' attacks -- undermining the trust-minimization property; (b) PoS concentrates power with existing token holders in a way PoW cannot; (c) SEC-adjacent scrutiny -- Gary Gensler suggested at one point that PoS tokens could be securities because staking looks like an investment contract; (d) PoW's energy cost is a FEATURE (external, real-world commitment) not a bug. T5: this debate is fundamental and unlikely to resolve empirically for decades. Bitcoin has stayed on proof-of-work as a core design principle -- calling it 'Nakamoto Consensus' and treating the energy expenditure as the security foundation. Ethereum bet the other way. Whether history vindicates one or the other, the argument itself teaches a real economic-engineering distinction: PoW imposes an EXTERNAL cost that anchors the network to physical reality; PoS keeps costs internal and depends on economic incentives among token holders. Further rungs: Vitalik Buterin (Ethereum's founder) has publicly favored PoS since Ethereum's early days; Cardano, Solana, and most post-2018 cryptocurrencies launched with PoS from the start; some altcoins (Litecoin, Dogecoin) remain on proof-of-work but are technical descendants of Bitcoin.

name: Bitcoin as a scarce digital commodity: the 21M cap in monetary theory
scope: Why the 21M cap is the deepest monetary claim Bitcoin makes. T1: throughout human history, EVERY commodity money has been chosen because it was DIFFICULT to produce more of -- gold from mines, seashells from beaches, rai stones from distant Palauan quarries requiring dangerous voyages. Difficulty of production was the property that made a good hold its value. T2: MENGER 1871 argued that money is the good with the highest MARKETABILITY -- the good with the deepest, most stable network of would-be trading partners. Marketability historically correlated with production difficulty because easy-to-produce goods flooded markets and lost value. T3: Bitcoin's 21 MILLION CAP is a form of production difficulty that has NEVER EXISTED BEFORE -- ABSOLUTE scarcity. Gold's supply grows about 1-2% per year through mining; silver similar; even the most disciplined fiat central bank grows money supply by several percent yearly. Bitcoin's issuance CURVE is knowable in advance and terminates. T4: this is the property that Saifedean Ammous calls STOCK-TO-FLOW SUPREMACY. Stock-to-flow is total existing supply divided by annual new production. Gold's stock-to-flow is roughly 60 (60 years of annual production to equal existing above-ground stock).
